RE: LD 73, An Act to Designate the Wood Turtle as the Official State Reptile
Dear Chair Baldacci, Chair Salisbury, and Members of the State and Local Government Committee:
My name is Ania Wright and I am Maine Audubon's Policy Advocate. Maine Audubon is a wildlife conservation nonprofit - we fulfill our mission to "conserve Maine wildlife and wildlife habitat" by engaging people of all ages in nature through a science-based approach to education, conservation, and advocacy. On behalf of Maine Audubon and our 30,000 members, supporters, and volunteers thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 73, An Act to Designate the Wood Turtle as the Official State Reptile.
It is with great enthusiasm that Maine Audubon supports the designation of the Wood Turtle (Glyptemys insculpta) as the official state reptile. Designating the Wood Turtle as the state reptile is a great opportunity for further public education of issues common with the species, which is at risk from the pet trade industry, road casualties, and habitat fragmentation. Furthermore, as we are the most forested state in the nation, the Wood Turtle is a fitting reptilian ambassador for the Pine Tree State.
The Wood Turtle is a species of special concern in Maine and an International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List Endangered Species. A species of special concern is any species of fish or wildlife that does not meet the criteria of an endangered or threatened species but is particularly vulnerable, and could easily become, an endangered, threatened, or extirpated species in Maine due to restricted distribution, low or declining numbers, specialized habitat needs or limits, or other factors.
The Wood Turtle is widespread across the state of Maine, unlike in our neighboring states, and found in aquatic, open field, and forest habitats. They use upland and forested areas in the late spring and into summer, can be found in slow moving rivers and lakes in warmer months, and during the winter hibernate underwater in slow-moving areas such as ponds, sheltered areas of rivers, or under logs and debris.

Maine Audubon has been instrumental in helping protect this long-lived but slow-to-reproduce species by reducing mortality from roadkill through various community science projects, and by facilitating movement along streams by replacing poorly functioning culverts with culverts that allow both aquatic and terrestrial passage of turtles and other animals. We also educate youth and adults about the importance of conserving turtles and their habitats through live animal presentations, interactive games, and other activities.
It is with great enthusiasm that we encourage the committee to support the designation of the Wood Turtle as the Maine state reptile. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Ania Wright Policy Advocate

10031832:
Brianna Carlson Caribou LD 73
Good Afternoon Representatives,
My name is Brianna Carlson, I am a resident of Caribou Maine. I am a turtle biologist, with a Bachelor's of Science in BIology Masters of Science in Marine Biology from The College of Charleston. In one of my first professional jobs, I conducted a reptile survey of the Padre Island National Seashore in Texas. I will never forget one of my coworkers confronting me as I held a beautiful hognose snake I'd caught, pulling out his knife and saying "when you're done, can we make it a good snake?" Indicating of course that the only good snake is a dead snake. Suffice it to say, not everyone is enamored with reptiles. Fast forward a few years and I had become an adjunct Instructor of Biology at Texas Southmost College. The great challenge of any instructor is to teach. But since I was tasked with teaching non-science majors, my challenge was to teach people to care about what I was teaching. I met this challenge by giving my students many projects to choose from to interact with the subject material on a personal level. Students left my class saying they were proud of what they had learned, including some of my education majors, who left feeling they knew better now how to teach. What you are being asked to consider today, creating a State Reptile, will give Mainers an opportunity to interact with the Wood Turtle in a new way. This vulnerable species, designated a species of special concern, is not an easy one to find. For five years I have been looking each summer on hikes and walks, and I finally saw one when it was brought to the Nylander Museum in Caribou as part of an Interpretive Program presented by the Chewonki Foundation this fall. Naming this elusive turtle, who resides throughout our state, the Maine State Reptile will give students of our state and others a new way to interact with this animal, and new cause to learn about them. Teachers, 4H and scout groups will teach young Mainers about this newly designated animal. It may be the first time many Mainers learn about the Wood Turtle, including discussions of ways to help protect the animal from vehicles and the pet trade industry. Ultimately, the benefits of naming the Wood Turtle as the State Reptile are best summarized by renowned oceanographer and educator Jacques Cousteau "We only protect what we love, we only love what we understand, and we only understand what we are taught." I ask you today to provide this designation of State Reptile to the Wood Turtle of Maine.

Good afternoon, Sen. Baldacci, Rep. Salisbury and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government. I am Laurie Osher, and I represent House District 25
in Orono. Thank you for the opportunity to present LD 7 3, An Act to Designate the Wood
Turtle as the Official State Reptile.
AS I shared in my previous testimony, I introduced this bill and its companion, LD 73, after a critter-loving constituent posted the question, "Why doesn't Maine have a State Amphibian?" It was a good question, so I consulted my friend and former colleague Dr. Aram Calhoun,
University of Maine professor emerita of wetland ecology. She consulted with her two co-editors of the book Maine Amphibians and Reptiles and suggested I sponsor legislation to create both a state amphibian: The Spring Peeper, and a state reptile: the wood turtle.
Unlike the spring peeper, the wood turtle is a species of special concern. While it does not yet
meet the criteria to be listed as endangered or threatened, it is vulnerable and could easily
become endangered if we do not act witl1 care. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:
"Th.e wood turtle once ranged widely across eastern landscapes characterized by meandering cobble-bottom streams and their surrounding fields andforests. Neither strictly aquatic nor terrestrial -- it lives both on land and in water -- the wood turtle is vulnerable to loss of both types of habitat. In addition to habitat loss andfiagmentation, wood turtles face threats from ~
agricultural machinery, invasive plants in nesting habitat, road-crossing mortality, degraded
"
water quality, disease, and illegal collection for the black-market pet trade.

Lukas Carlson Caribou LD 73
Good Afternoon,
My name is Luke, and I like reptiles. I used to live in Texas, where there were lots of reptiles, but many were very unsafe. I had to know about them to keep safe. Here in Maine, none of the reptiles will send you to the hospital, but I think that means that people learn less about them. Designating the Wood Turtle as the State Reptile would encourage more people to learn about this amazing turtle. It would be great to have more learning opportunities to teach about turtles in Maine. Last summer at camp, I found a turtle and showed it to another scout. It was really neat to catch a turtle, and we had a fun story to share that night around the campfire. Other scouts were excited and wanted to see a turtle, too. Many kids like animals and want to see more of them. Wouldn't it be great if designating the Wood Turtle as the Maine State Reptile helped its population recover and encounters with them became a more regular occurrence. Please make the Wood Turtle the Maine State Reptile.
Thank you.

TESTIMONY OF THE
DEPARTMENT OF INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT
IN SUPPORT OF L.D. 73
"An Act to Designate the Wood Turtle as the Official State Reptile"
SPONSORED BY: Representative OSHER of Orono. COSPONSORED BY: Senator BRENNER of Cumberland and Representative: ANKELES of
Brunswick
DATE OF HEARING: Monday, February 3, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the State and Local Government Committee. I am Phillip DeMaynadier, Wildlife Diversity Section Supen/isor at the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, speaking on behalf of the Department, in support
of L.D. 73.
This bill designates the wood turtle as the official state reptile.
Many states designate official species (e.g., state tree, flower, bird, etc.) as a way of showing
pride in their natural heritage and for raising public awareness of a particular species group. For
example, the 131" legislature recently designated the Pink-edged Sulphur as the official state
butterfly. This bill would designate the Wood Turtle (1 of 6 native [nonmarine] turtles in Maine)
as the official state reptile of Maine. The Department recommends support for this designation as Maine does not have a state reptile, and to our knowledge no other U.S. jurisdiction has
designated this species. The Wood Turtle is also a good choice because it is: exceptionally
attractive, distributed statewide, and closely associated with clean rivers flowing through intact forested watersheds, which remain thankfully abundant in Maine.
I would be glad to answer any questions at this time or during the work session.
